newsitem.title: USA: Group wants Wall Street tax proposals dropped.
newsitem.headline: Group wants Wall Street tax proposals dropped.

text.p: The Securities Industry Association has asked the Clinton administration to drop tax proposals it advanced last year that would raise revenue by closing tax loopholes on Wall Street.

In a letter to Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, SIA President Marc Lackritz said such proposals would not add revenue, but would discourage investment by raising the cost of capital and limiting financing alternatives for businesses.
"These proposals have been unfairly characterized as a package to eliminate 'corporate welfare,'" Lackritz said in the letter dated Monday but released Tuesday.
"The transactions, however, are legitimte corporate financing techniques, and proposing to alter them to raise revenue would have an immediate and negative effect on the capital markets," he said.
An administration official said earlier this month that President Clinton is expected to resurrect the proposals in his fiscal year 1998 budget to be unveiled next month.

The proposals include measures that would discourage the issuance of 100-year bonds and the use of hybrid debt/equity financing mechanisms by corporations as well as one that ends the scheme in which capital gains taxes are deferred when investors short-sell shares of stock they already owns.
If the proposals are resurrected, Lackritz urged the administration to seek to make them effective no earlier than the "date of enactment."
"Retroactive or immediate effective dates would send shock waves through the capital markets," he said.
